bibliographic.authors: Po-Kai Chang (a); Ta-Chih Hsiao (a,b,c,*). a Graduate Institute of Environmental Engineering, National Taiwan University; b Research Centre for Environmental Changes, Academia Sinica; c Institute of Atomic and Molecular Sciences, Academia Sinica
bibliographic.year: 2026 (received 25 Sep 2025; revised 31 Dec 2025; accepted 1 Jan 2026; available online 2 Jan 2026)
bibliographic.title: Evaluation of spatial distribution of cancer risk induced by traffic-related ultrafine particles within an urban microenvironment in New Taipei City, Taiwan
bibliographic.citation: Chang P-K, Hsiao T-C (2026). Evaluation of spatial distribution of cancer risk induced by traffic-related ultrafine particles within an urban microenvironment in New Taipei City, Taiwan. Journal of Hazardous Materials 502:141024. doi:10.1016/j.jhazmat.2026.141024
bibliographic.funding: Taiwan National Science and Technology Council, grant NSTC 114-2221-E-002-075-MY3 (Hsiao declares this support as a financial interest). Authors used OpenAI ChatGPT for readability and language only.
bibliographic.openAccess: unknown (page 1 footer: 'All rights are reserved, including those for text and data mining, AI training, and similar technologies'; no open-access licence printed). Data availability: 'Data will be made available on request.' Supplementary data exist but were not available to the checker.

studyDesign: Pure modelling study; no new field measurements. Domain: 1.2 km x 1.2 km target area in Zhonghe District, New Taipei City, inside a circular computational domain of 800 m radius (p.3; the square's half-diagonal is about 850 m so this is loosely described). Dense mixed commercial/residential, building coverage about 71 %, Yonghe/Zhonghe population density about 24,600 per km2; contains arterials, elevated expressways, an interchange, a freeway segment and schools (p.2-3). Flow: steady RANS, standard k-epsilon, COMSOL, building-resolved, about 5 m horizontal and about 1 m vertical grid near ground; log-law inlet with roughness length 2 m; winds from Datun Mountain station (1079 m): 9.79 m/s winter from 60 deg, 4.30 m/s summer from 240 deg (p.3-4). Particles: size-resolved convection-diffusion for 20-100 nm (Brownian diffusion, Stokes-corrected turbulent diffusion, settling), one-way coupled, size constant, linear so sources add; a CDM-versus-DPM check for 50 and 100 nm is in the Supplement (p.5). Emissions: four uniform line/surface sources (urban roads, elevated expressways at about 15 m, interchanges, freeways) = hourly counts for three classes (motorcycles, light-duty, heavy-duty) x size-resolved EF from a Taipei tunnel experiment (inlet-outlet increase; includes exhaust and non-exhaust); peak 07-09 and 17-19, off-peak 12-14 (p.5-6). Dose and risk: SA_UFP with age-specific MPPD deposition for ages 3, 9, 21 at heights 0.9, 1.2, 1.6 m; ELCR = (IR x T / BW) x SFm x Cf x SA_UFP with SFm 1.0e-3 (peak) and 7.9e-4 (off-peak) kg day/mg from ref 51 and Cf 6.6e-13 mg/nm2 (p.6). Scenarios: 2 seasons x peak/off-peak x 3 ages. Validation: wind speed/direction versus two on-site stations (quantitative for dominant-bin speed); particle fields only qualitatively (relative ordering) against the authors' earlier measurements, details in Supplement (p.7-8). No electrification or fleet scenario. The word 'scooter' does not appear; vehicle class is 'motorcycles' and fuel type is not stated.

findings.claim: The study is a CFD model of one 1.2 x 1.2 km area in Zhonghe, not a measurement campaign.
findings.value: 1.2 km x 1.2 km domain; about 5 m horizontal and about 1 m vertical grid near ground; building coverage about 71 %
findings.quote: microscale computational fluid dynamics (CFD) simulations (1.2 × 1.2 km2 domain with about 5 m horizontal resolution near the ground)
findings.caveats: Single domain; authors say ranking of factors 'can vary with the size of the target area and with receptor location' (p.13). Text says the square target area is enclosed in a circular computational domain of 800 m radius (p.3); a 1.2 km square has a half-diagonal of about 850 m, so the description is internally loose (maps are circular).
findings.useOnSite: The authors modelled a 1.2 km square of dense Zhonghe streets at about 5 m resolution.
findings.checkerNote: Quote and numbers verified (p.1, p.3 for 71 %, p.4 for grid). Added the circle-versus-square oddity as a caveat.

findings.claim: The simulated wind field was compared with two on-site stations; speed error at the dominant direction bin was small, direction error up to 50 deg at the open weather station.
findings.value: Speed at dominant direction bin: RMSE 0.29 m/s, NMB -3.7 %; direction RMSE below 20 deg at measurement station (4 m), up to 50 deg at weather station (17 m). Simulated station speeds: weather station about 1.84 m/s winter, 2.32 m/s summer; measurement station 1.54 and 1.69 m/s; judged to 'correspond well' with observed 1-3 m/s ranges
findings.kind: modelled (compared with measured wind data from the authors' earlier study)
findings.quote: CFD results yield a RMSE of 0.29 m/s and a normalized mean bias (NMB) of − 3.7 %
findings.caveats: Validation is of wind only, not of particles. The RMSE/NMB is for the dominant directional bin only; the other comparison is a loose match to a 1-3 m/s range read from wind roses. Authors attribute direction deviations to 'localized obstructions or model simplifications'.
findings.useOnSite: Simulated winds matched on-site wind speed within about 0.3 m/s (RMSE) in the dominant direction bin.
findings.checkerNote: Number and page correct. Changed kind from 'measured' to modelled-vs-measured comparison, and added that the RMSE is for the dominant bin only and that station-level agreement is described loosely.

findings.claim: Particle-concentration validation is qualitative in the main text: the model reproduces ranking across locations with 'modest discrepancies' in absolute values; no validation statistics are printed.
findings.value: No R2, RMSE or NMB for particle concentrations in main text (Supplement referenced)
findings.quote: While modest discrepancies exist in absolute particle concentrations, the model accurately reproduces the relative ordering of concentrations across receptor locations
findings.caveats: Supplementary Material was not available to the checker or reader; statistics may be there. The authors also say it 'aligns well with in-situ data at the measurement station'; the comparison data are the authors' own earlier measurements [31,59].
findings.useOnSite: Do not quote a validation accuracy for concentrations; say the model reproduced the relative ordering of sites.
findings.checkerNote: Page corrected from 9 to 8 (the sentence is on printed page 8, before the Section 3.3 heading). Content confirmed; no statistics in the main text.

findings.claim: Vehicles are grouped into only three classes (motorcycles, light-duty, heavy-duty); emission factors are size-resolved 20-100 nm from a Taipei tunnel experiment.
findings.value: 3 vehicle categories; EF in particles/km for 20-100 nm; numeric EFs and traffic counts only in Supplement (Fig S3, Table S3-S4); traffic counts from the authors' earlier study [31] and the Ministry of Transportation and Communications
findings.quote: vehicles were grouped into three categories: motorcycles, light-duty vehicles, and heavy-duty vehicles
findings.caveats: No emission-factor number for motorcycles appears in the main text; no share of emissions by vehicle class is reported; fuel or engine type of motorcycles is not stated; the word scooter does not appear anywhere in the paper.
findings.useOnSite: The model uses a tunnel-derived size spectrum per vehicle class including motorcycles, but the main text reports no motorcycle-specific numbers.
findings.checkerNote: Content right; page corrected from 5-6 to 6 (the sentence is on p.6; Eq. 15 is p.5). Added that the paper never says 'scooter' and that counts come from ref 31 and MOTC.

findings.claim: The tunnel-derived emission factors mix exhaust and non-exhaust sources, so modelled particles are not purely tailpipe.
findings.value: n/a
findings.quote: they reflect the combined contribution of exhaust and non-exhaust traffic emissions, including brake wear, tire wear, and resuspension
findings.caveats: Weakens a strict 'tailpipe' attribution. EFs were inferred from the net rise between tunnel inlet and outlet and include initial dilution and cooling of exhaust particles.
findings.useOnSite: The paper models traffic particles generally; it does not isolate tailpipe emissions.
findings.checkerNote: Page corrected from 5 to 6. Quote verified.

findings.claim: Only 20-100 nm particles are modelled; particles under 20 nm are excluded, so absolute UFP and risk are probably underestimated.
findings.value: Window 20-100 nm; authors cite literature that particles below 30 nm typically contribute about 20 % or less of LDSA
findings.quote: total UFP number emissions are therefore likely underestimated to some extent
findings.caveats: The 20 % figure is cited from refs 48-50, not measured here. Authors also say the effect on SA_UFP and ELCR 'is expected to be limited' and spatial patterns unlikely to change much (p.6).
findings.useOnSite: The authors state their model may underestimate absolute UFP because it omits particles below 20 nm.
findings.checkerNote: Verified; added the authors' own view that the truncation effect is expected to be limited.

findings.claim: Ground-level urban roads gave the highest and most confined near-road lung-deposited UFP surface area, about 40 um2/cm3 at kerb and sidewalk, decaying within a few tens of metres.
findings.value: about 40 μm2/cm3 SA_UFP at curbside/sidewalk (z = 1.6 m), peak hours, urban-road source alone
findings.quote: SAUFP maxima are concentrated at curbside and sidewalk locations (approximately 40 μm2/cm3) and decay rapidly within a few tens of meters from the roadway
findings.caveats: Modelled at 1.6 m (adult breathing height); 'a few tens of metres' is qualitative with no distance-decay table; Fig 6 shows maps only. The authors say the pattern is consistent with earlier near-road observations [54,55].
findings.useOnSite: In the model, kerbside and sidewalk air beside busy streets had about 40 μm2/cm3 of lung-deposited UFP surface area from urban-road traffic, falling off within a few tens of metres.
findings.checkerNote: Quote, number, page verified against p.8.

findings.claim: The 3D simulations show pronounced hotspots at major intersections where plumes from two crossing streets converge.
findings.value: Qualitative; urban-road SA_UFP peaks about 40 μm2/cm3 'confined to narrow street-canyon bands and intersection hotspots'
findings.quote: pronounced hotspots at major intersections, where plumes from two crossing streets converge and lead to local accumulation of UFPs
findings.caveats: No separate intersection concentration number; emissions are a uniform per-road flux (Eq. 15) with no signal cycle, queue or idling, so the intersection effect arises from geometry and plume convergence only.
findings.useOnSite: The model finds that intersections accumulate particles from two crossing streets; it does not model red-light queues or idling.
findings.checkerNote: Verified. The no-queue/no-idling statement is the checker's reading of Eq. 15 and the stated uniform-flux assumption; the paper never mentions queues, idling or signals.

findings.claim: At a busy T-intersection (location F), urban roads were the primary risk source in all scenarios, with adult ELCR about 1.7e-4 in winter peak.
findings.value: ELCR about 1.7 × 10-4 (21-year-old adult, winter peak, location F)
findings.quote: Winter peak conditions yield total ELCR of about 1.7 × 10− 4
findings.locator: Section 3.5; Fig. 9 (Fig. 9 is p.12, text on p.13)
findings.caveats: Adult at 1.6 m; one receptor point; modelled risk indicator, not incidence. From Fig. 9 (read from figure, approximate) F summer peak is lower, roughly 1.1e-4, and off-peak bars are lower still; in summer 'elevated sources play only a minor role'.
findings.useOnSite: At a modelled busy T-intersection, local traffic on the urban roads, not elevated roads, drove the modelled risk for an adult.
findings.checkerNote: Page corrected from 12-13 to 13 for the F text (figure on p.12). Added the summer value read from Fig. 9, flagged approximate.

findings.claim: Elevated expressways (about 15 m emission height) give broader footprints and lower near-ground intensity, but building downwash can create secondary ground-level hotspots downwind.
findings.value: Expressway plume about 30-40 μm2/cm3 over a wide sector in winter; local maxima up to about 60 μm2/cm3 near domain edge in summer
findings.quote: Elevated plumes are deflected and entrained downward by facade-induced downwash and wake effects, which funnel particles toward ground-level microenvironments
findings.caveats: Complicates a 'low-level tailpipe at the kerb' story: part of the modelled pedestrian-height burden comes from elevated roads.
findings.useOnSite: Not all modelled exposure comes from kerb-side street traffic; elevated roads also contribute at pedestrian height in places.
findings.checkerNote: Verified.

findings.claim: Interchange and freeway sources had strongly season-dependent footprints; the freeway segment had the weakest near-ground impact.
findings.value: Interchange: generally below 20 μm2/cm3 (winter), above 30 across the southern sector (summer). Freeway: winter peak approaches 55 in a narrow plume only a few tens of metres long; summer max around 20
findings.quote: concentrations exceed 30 μm2/cm3 across the southern sector
findings.caveats: Source-specific maps only.
findings.useOnSite: n/a (technical detail)
findings.checkerNote: Verified.

findings.claim: Domain-mean lung-deposited UFP surface area at 1.6 m during peak hours was 15 um2/cm3 (winter) and 31 um2/cm3 (summer), with local maxima of 65 and 80 um2/cm3 beneath the expressways.
findings.value: Peak: mean 15 (winter) / 31 (summer) μm2/cm3, 'spatial variability of about 15'; max 65 / 80. Off-peak maxima about 45 / 60. Off-peak means are not unambiguously stated
findings.quote: the spatial mean SAUFP during winter peak hours is 15 μm2/cm3, with spatial variability of about 15 μm2/cm3. The local maximum reaches 65 μm2/cm3
findings.caveats: Maxima occur near urban roads located beneath expressways (combined urban-road and elevated contribution), not urban road alone. 'Spatial variability' is not defined as a standard deviation. The off-peak sentence literally reads 'The spatial mean SAUFP decreases 10 μm2/cm3 in winter and 21 μm2/cm3 in summer'; read literally that would be a drop of 10, which conflicts with the stated 32 % reduction. Reading 10 and 21 as the off-peak levels is consistent (15 x 0.68 = 10.2; 31 x 0.68 = 21.1) but is an inference.
findings.useOnSite: The model gives an area average of 15 to 31 μm2/cm3 at rush hour, with hotspots roughly 2.6 to 4.3 times the area mean (80/31, 65/15).
findings.checkerNote: Peak figures confirmed. Off-peak means 10 and 21 downgraded to 'inferred'; paper wording is ambiguous. Replaced 'two to four times' with the computed range. Described 'spatial variability' as undefined.

findings.claim: Average emission intensity about 28 % lower off-peak gave domain-average SA_UFP about 32 % lower, with local reductions above 35-40 % near major urban roads.
findings.value: Emission intensity about 28 % lower (average across the four line sources); domain-averaged SA_UFP about 32 % lower; local reductions can exceed 35-40 % near major urban roads; smaller reductions in well-ventilated downwind sectors
findings.quote: the average emission intensity during off-peak hours is approximately 28 % lower than during peak periods, yet local SAUFP reductions can exceed 35–40 % near major urban roads
findings.caveats: This is a time-of-day traffic-volume change, not an electrification scenario; it does not distinguish vehicle type or fuel. Because the transport equation is linear (p.6), a reduction larger than the emission cut is not a nonlinear response; the checker reads it as a consequence of source weighting and spatial pattern (not explained by the authors). Off-peak is 12:00-14:00 versus 07-09 and 17-19.
findings.useOnSite: In the model, cutting traffic emissions by about 28 % cut average UFP surface-area exposure by about 32 % and by more than 35 % beside major roads. This was a traffic-volume change, not a switch to electric vehicles.
findings.checkerNote: Numbers and quotes confirmed. Corrected page attribution (28 % and 35-40 % statements are on p.10, 32 % on p.8). Removed the implication of a 'more-than-proportional' response; the model is linear, so that is a weighting effect.

findings.claim: The authors compare their results with other roadside studies reporting LDSA of 30-50 um2/cm3 in peak hours and 20-40 um2/cm3 midday.
findings.value: 30-50 μm2/cm3 (peak, cited); 20-40 μm2/cm3 (midday, cited)
findings.quote: Previous roadside studies in traffic-dominated urban areas have reported LDSA concentrations on the order of 30–50 μm2/cm3 during peak hours
findings.caveats: Cited from refs 60-62 (Los Angeles, urban Europe, Guangzhou per reference titles), not Taiwan. Not this paper's results.
findings.useOnSite: Modelled values are of the same order as roadside values reported elsewhere (cited by the authors).
findings.checkerNote: Verified against p.8 and reference titles.

findings.claim: Using the authors' earlier PMF analysis at the same site, traffic-related SA_UFP was more than nine times that of regional background and of cooking/secondary aerosol.
findings.value: more than nine times (two comparisons)
findings.quote: the mean SAUFP from traffic-related factors was more than nine times higher than that from the regional background factor and also more than nine times higher than that from the cooking/secondary factor
findings.caveats: From the authors' earlier study (ref 31, titled 'Particulate matter in a motorcycle-dominated urban area'), reconverted to SA_UFP; the traffic factors are all traffic, not scooters specifically; this paper does not say what share of those factors is motorcycles.
findings.useOnSite: At this site, the authors' earlier source apportionment attributes most lung-deposited UFP surface area to traffic.
findings.checkerNote: Verified on p.11.

findings.claim: Modelled peak adult ELCR maxima were about 2.2e-4 (winter) and 3.0e-4 (summer).
findings.value: 21-year-old adult, peak hours: max about 2.2 × 10-4 winter; 3.0 × 10-4 summer; domain-averaged adult ELCR about 3.2 × 10-5 to 1.3 × 10-4 across seasons and traffic scenarios
findings.quote: Peak adult ELCR reaches about 2.2 × 10− 4 in winter and 3.0 × 10− 4 in summer
findings.caveats: Deterministic point estimates, no confidence intervals. Potential risk indicator from a composite slope factor; not a prediction of incidence (authors).
findings.useOnSite: The authors' model gives a maximum adult lifetime excess cancer risk indicator of order 2-3 in 10,000 at the worst locations; they call it a potential risk indicator, not a prediction.
findings.checkerNote: Verified (p.1, p.11, p.12 for the domain-average range). Fig. 8 whiskers agree.

findings.claim: 9-year-old children had the highest modelled ELCR, about 4.5e-4 winter peak and 6.5e-4 summer peak, versus adult 2.2e-4 and 3.0e-4.
findings.value: 9-year-old max: about 4.5 × 10-4 (winter peak), approaching 6.5 × 10-4 (summer peak); adults 2.2 and 3.0; 3-year-old below 9-year-old; 21-year-old lowest. Ratio child:adult maximum about 2.1-2.2 (checker arithmetic)
findings.quote: the winter maximum ELCR for this group is approximately 4.5 × 10− 4, while the summer peak approaches 6.5 × 10− 4
findings.caveats: Values are maxima over grid points, no uncertainty ranges. Children's excess comes from assumed inhalation rate, body weight and MPPD deposition, not observed outcomes. Child receptor evaluated at 1.2 m (9 y) and 0.9 m (3 y); main-text maps are at 1.6 m. In Fig. 8 the violin means (circles, read from figure, approximate) at peak are roughly 1.0 (3 y), 1.2 (9 y), 0.6 (adult) x10-4 in winter and roughly 2.1, 2.5, 1.3 x10-4 in summer; most winter grid points lie below about 2e-4. No elderly group, riders or workers modelled.
findings.useOnSite: In this model, a 9-year-old at the worst locations had about twice the lifetime excess cancer risk indicator of an adult, because children breathe more per kilogram and deposit more particles in the lungs.
findings.checkerNote: Maxima and quote verified. Reader's 'medians roughly 0.3-1.5e-4 for children' was inaccurate against Fig. 8 (summer peak circles are about 2.1-2.5e-4); replaced with figure-read means, flagged approximate.

findings.claim: The authors attribute the child excess to higher inhalation rate per unit body weight and the highest alveolar deposition efficiency for 20-100 nm particles in 9-year-olds.
findings.value: n/a (MPPD, Fig S5)
findings.quote: this age group has the highest alveolar deposition efficiency for particles in the 20–100 nm range
findings.caveats: MPPD Age-Specific 5-Lobe model; only ages 3, 9 and 21 modelled. Adults lowest 'because of their higher body weight and slightly lower deposition fractions'.
findings.useOnSite: The model's child excess is a physiological dose effect (breathing rate per body weight and lung deposition), not a measured health outcome.
findings.checkerNote: Verified.

findings.claim: Authors place modelled adult ELCR in the range of other urban UFP studies and indoor cooking, far below smoking, and say some locations exceed the US EPA 1e-6 to 1e-4 band, especially for children.
findings.value: Other urban UFP studies 2.5e-5 to 2.0e-4 'and even higher under certain building configurations'; indoor cooking 1.01e-4; smoking 2-6e-1; US EPA band 1e-6 to 1e-4
findings.quote: modeled ELCR values at some locations exceed the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency’s suggested acceptable risk threshold of 10− 6 to 10− 4
findings.locator: Section 3.4 end (p.12); p.13 conclusion ('fall above the 10-6-10-4 band')
findings.caveats: 'Acceptable risk threshold' is the authors' wording. The values 'exceed' the band, meaning above its 1e-4 upper end, not merely above 1e-6. The comparison values are cited; the cooking value used the same SA-based method (ref 5). Ref 51 (same group) is one of two sources for the 'other studies' range. The paper gives no regulatory UFP unit risk.
findings.useOnSite: Do not frame results as breaching a legal limit; the paper itself says UFP carcinogenic potency 'remains subject to scientific uncertainty'.
findings.checkerNote: Page corrected from 11-12 to 12. Reader's 'above the lower end of the band' was wrong; the authors mean exceeding the band (above 1e-4). Added that ref 51 is also a comparator source.

findings.claim: At two modelled schools, adult ELCR ranged from about 2.7e-5 to 1.8e-4 depending on season and wind position.
findings.value: School B winter peak about 1.2 × 10-4; school A winter peak about 2.7 × 10-5 (78 % lower, downwind); school A summer peak 1.8 × 10-4; B summer 8.1 × 10-5 excluding urban-road contribution (57 % lower)
findings.quote: At A, which is located downwind, particles are diluted during transport and the ELCR decreases to about 2.7 × 10− 5, representing a reduction of 78 %
findings.caveats: Values are for 21-year-old adults (Fig 9 caption), not children. Schools driven mainly by elevated sources rather than adjacent urban roads. The 8.1e-5 at B excludes urban roads. The paper infers children would be higher but computes no child values for these sites. 1.8e-4 to 8.1e-5 is a 55 % drop by arithmetic; authors say about 57 %.
findings.useOnSite: Modelled adult-equivalent risk near schools varied several-fold with wind direction and building layout and was driven largely by elevated roads.
findings.checkerNote: Verified, including Fig. 9 bar heights.

findings.claim: Along the east-west arterial beneath an expressway, adult ELCR reached about 2.4e-4 (site D, winter peak) and 2.8e-4 (site E, summer peak); off-peak at D stayed above 1.3e-4.
findings.value: D winter peak about 2.4 × 10-4; D off-peak above 1.3 × 10-4; E summer peak about 2.8 × 10-4
findings.quote: even during off-peak periods the ELCR remains above 1.3 × 10− 4, indicating that the canyon geometry sustains high exposure despite reduced emissions
findings.caveats: Adults; combined urban-road plus expressway contribution (see added finding on the urban-road share); one point each.
findings.useOnSite: Street canyons below elevated roads kept high modelled exposure even when traffic was lower.
findings.checkerNote: Verified.

findings.claim: An open sports park had mean adult ELCR below 1e-4 in all scenarios, but elevated sources accounted for a large share of it.
findings.value: below 1 × 10-4 (location C)
findings.quote: adults and children gathering in nominally “clean” open spaces may still experience non-negligible UFP-related cancer risk driven by traffic emissions transported from some distance away
findings.caveats: Adult values only; 'non-negligible' is author wording.
findings.useOnSite: Open space dilutes street-level plumes quickly, but not entirely.
findings.checkerNote: Verified.

findings.claim: Authors conclude a single monitoring value cannot represent the microenvironment because of steep gradients.
findings.value: Mean 15, variability about 15, max 65 μm2/cm3 (winter peak)
findings.quote: indicate that a single monitoring value is insufficient to represent the entire urban microenvironment
findings.caveats: Based on model output.
findings.useOnSite: Exposure varies a lot over short distances, so fixed monitors may miss hotspots.
findings.checkerNote: Verified.

findings.claim: Receptors were evaluated at 0.9 m (age 3), 1.2 m (age 9) and 1.6 m (adult); the paper reports no concentration-versus-height result.
findings.quote: horizontal slices were extracted at z = 0.9, 1.2, and 1.6 m, representing the breathing heights of 3-, 9-, and 21-year-old receptors
findings.caveats: No stroller height and no vertical decay in the main text (Supplement not seen). Question 3 on decay with height is not answered by the main text.
findings.useOnSite: Do not claim a height gradient from this paper.
findings.checkerNote: Verified.

findings.claim: Summer gave higher modelled peak ELCR than winter, due to wind regime, though the winter background wind was stronger.
findings.value: Adult max 3.0e-4 vs 2.2e-4 (about 35 % higher); child max 6.5e-4 vs 4.5e-4 (40-45 % higher); domain mean SA 31 vs 15 μm2/cm3
findings.quote: For adults, the summer maximum ELCR (3.0 × 10− 4) is roughly 35 % higher than the winter maximum (2.2 × 10− 4)
findings.caveats: Only one idealised steady wind per season (9.79 m/s from 60 deg; 4.30 m/s from 240 deg) at a hilltop station, not street level. Authors say the difference arises from where interchange and freeway plumes go.
findings.useOnSite: n/a
findings.checkerNote: Verified (p.11; wind inputs p.4).

findings.claim: The cancer toxicity value is a composite slope factor for traffic particles from a Taipei trace-metal study, not a regulatory UFP unit risk.
findings.value: SFm = 1.0 × 10-3 kg·day/mg (peak) and 7.9 × 10-4 kg·day/mg (off-peak); Cf = 6.6 × 10-13 mg/nm2 (from ref 5)
findings.quote: The SFm values during peak (1.0 ×10− 3 kg⋅day/mg) and off-peak hours (7.9 ×10− 4 kg⋅day/mg) were based on the previously reported experimental results [51]
findings.caveats: Ref 51 title: 'Real-time Assessment of PM1.0-bound Trace Metal Cancer Risk through High-Resolution GED-ICP-MS and Integrated ELCR Analysis' (Chou et al., J Hazard Mater 494, 138711, 2025; Hsiao is a co-author). SFm differs peak versus off-peak (peak is about 27 % higher; off-peak about 21 % lower), so part of the peak/off-peak ELCR contrast reflects an assumed composition change as well as concentration. Inhalation rate and body weight are in Supplement Table S5; the exposure time T is not stated in the main text.
findings.useOnSite: The cancer-risk numbers rest on a slope factor derived from trace-metal composition of Taipei traffic particles; the paper itself says UFP carcinogenic potency is uncertain.
findings.checkerNote: Removed the reader's parenthetical claim that no regulator has a UFP unit risk (not in the paper; reader flagged it themselves). Added ref 51 title and that T is not given. Numbers and page verified.

findings.claim: The authors state the ELCR values are potential risk indicators, not predictions of incidence, and that UFP carcinogenic potency remains scientifically uncertain.
findings.value: n/a
findings.quote: the ELCR values reported here should be interpreted as potential risk indicators rather than direct predictions of cancer incidence
findings.caveats: Section 4: 'suitable for comparing relative spatial patterns and vulnerable locations, rather than as precise predictions of absolute cancer incidence.'
findings.useOnSite: Quote the authors' own caveat next to any risk number.
findings.checkerNote: Verified.

findings.claim: The authors state evidence for UFP carcinogenicity is more limited and less consistent than for PM2.5, while evidence for respiratory and cardiovascular effects is increasing.
findings.value: n/a
findings.quote: although the overall evidence base remains more limited and less consistent than for PM2.5 [1,2]
findings.caveats: Cited from refs 1-2; no health-effect data produced here.
findings.useOnSite: The paper offers no new evidence on what UFP do in the body.
findings.checkerNote: Verified.

findings.claim: Authors recommend priority traffic control near sensitive receptors, facade or kerbside measures at canyon hotspots and below viaducts, and time-of-day traffic management; they do not model or mention electrification.
findings.value: n/a; also 'reducing traffic emissions is the most direct way to improve air quality and lower exposure' (p.13)
findings.quote: priority control of traffic near sensitive receptors, localized curbside or facade measures at canyon hotspots and below viaducts, and time-of-day traffic management
findings.caveats: No electric vehicle scenario; no fleet-composition scenario. The words electric and gasoline do not appear in the paper.
findings.useOnSite: The paper supports reducing traffic emissions in general but contains no electrification scenario.
findings.checkerNote: Verified; searched the text for 'electric', 'gasoline', 'scooter': none.

findings.claim: Authors conclude emission strength and seasonal wind set the overall level of risk, while source height and morphology mostly redistribute it.
findings.value: n/a
findings.quote: emission strength and seasonal wind conditions primarily set the overall level of UFP-related cancer risk while source height and urban morphology mainly redistribute this risk in space
findings.caveats: Stated for this case study only; the 'emission strength' evidence is the peak versus off-peak comparison.
findings.useOnSite: In this study, emission strength was the first-order driver of exposure.
findings.checkerNote: Verified.

findings.claim: Fig. 8 shows that high ELCR applies to a minority of grid points; the winter distribution is concentrated below 1e-4 while summer is broader.
findings.value: Text: winter ELCR 'most values falling below 1 × 10-4'; summer 'broader and more uniform'. Figure-read (approximate) violin means at peak: winter 3 y about 1.0, 9 y about 1.2, adult about 0.6 x10-4; summer 3 y about 2.1, 9 y about 2.5, adult about 1.3 x10-4
findings.quote: In contrast, the winter ELCR distribution is more concentrated, with most values falling below 1 × 10− 4
findings.caveats: Figure values read by eye from the violin/box plot and are approximate; the text sentence does not say which age group. Means across all receptor grid points in the domain, not residents.
findings.useOnSite: Most of the modelled area is well below the maxima; the headline maxima apply to hotspot locations.
findings.checkerNote: Added: reader mis-stated the child violin medians and omitted that the winter statement is explicitly for winter only.

findings.claim: The main text does not give the daily exposure time T or exposure duration used in the ELCR equation, so the absolute risk magnitude cannot be reproduced from the main text.
findings.value: Eq. 16: ELCR = (IR × T / BW) × SFm × Cf × SA_UFP; T 'daily exposure time (h/day)'; IR and BW in Table S5 (Supplement)
findings.quote: IR is the inhalation rate (m3/h), T is the daily exposure time (h/day)
findings.caveats: Eq. 16 has no explicit lifetime or years-of-exposure term; no time-activity, indoor-outdoor penetration or mobility (authors, p.13). The ELCR therefore assumes the receptor stands at the grid point at the stated T.
findings.useOnSite: Treat the ELCR values as relative indicators of where and for whom; do not present them as what a resident's risk is.
findings.checkerNote: Added: important to sceptical readers; the paper's own limitations paragraph (p.13) lists time-activity and indoor-outdoor penetration as not resolved.

findings.claim: In Fig. 9, ground-level urban roads supply only part of the adult ELCR at the two canyon-under-viaduct hotspots D and E, but all of it at intersection F.
findings.value: Figure-read (approximate, bar colours per legend): D winter peak urban-road about 1.1 of about 2.4 x10-4; E summer peak urban-road about 1.0 of about 2.8 x10-4; F winter peak entirely urban-road about 1.7 x10-4
findings.quote: Urban roads and the expressway together account for most of this risk
findings.caveats: Read by eye from stacked bars; text gives only 'most' for D and says F is dominated by urban roads. Adults only.
findings.useOnSite: Even at the worst canyon sites, roughly half or more of the modelled adult risk came from the elevated expressway or interchange, not the street itself.

limitations: Authors: steady-state winds for one representative winter and one summer condition; no transient wind, traffic-induced turbulence or atmospheric stability; no particle-to-flow feedback (p.13).
Authors: particle size constant during transport; no condensation, evaporation or coagulation (p.13).
Authors: only 20-100 nm modelled; total UFP number emissions 'likely underestimated to some extent' (p.13); elsewhere they expect limited effect on spatial patterns (p.6).

Authors: ELCR relies on 'a composite cancer slope factor derived for traffic related ultrafine particles in Taipei' and simplified exposure assumptions; time-activity, indoor-outdoor penetration and individual susceptibility not resolved; values are 'potential risks under the assumed scenarios', not 'precise predictions of absolute cancer incidence' (p.13).
Authors: carcinogenic potency of UFPs 'remains subject to scientific uncertainty' (p.11); evidence base for UFP carcinogenicity 'more limited and less consistent than for PM2.5' (p.2).
Authors: ranking of factors 'can vary with the size of the target area and with receptor location' (p.13).
Authors list three assumptions: particle size unchanged, particles uniformly emitted from each line source, all particles spherical (p.6); coarse particles taken as negligible (p.6).
Checker: main text gives no particle-concentration validation statistics; only wind has RMSE/NMB (dominant bin). Supplement not available.
Checker: emissions are uniform surface fluxes with no signals, queues or idling, so red-light effects are not modelled; paper does not mention them.
Checker: traffic counts and emission factors are only in the Supplement; the main text has no vehicle-class emission numbers or shares.
Checker: no confidence intervals, uncertainty ranges or sensitivity ranges on any SA_UFP or ELCR value; exposure time T not stated in the main text.

Checker: data 'available on request'; the corresponding author holds the funding grant; the slope factor comes from a study (ref 51) co-authored by Hsiao and the PMF source apportionment from the authors' earlier work (ref 31).
complications: Scooters are not separately analysed: motorcycles are one of three vehicle classes; no motorcycle emission factor, no motorcycle share of UFP or of modelled concentration, and no statement of whether they are gasoline or electric. The paper cannot be cited for 'scooters cause X % of the UFP'.

Sources are resolved by road type, not vehicle type. Elevated roads matter: the highest maxima (65 and 80 um2/cm3) are near urban roads beneath expressways, and schools and the park are driven largely by elevated sources.
Emission factors from a tunnel include non-exhaust particles (brake, tyre, resuspension); a switch to electric would not remove those components, and the paper cannot say how much they contribute.
No electrification or fleet-change scenario; the only emission-reduction evidence is peak versus off-peak traffic (about 28 % lower emissions, about 32 % lower mean SA_UFP).
No red-light queue or idling analysis; intersection hotspots come from plume convergence from crossing streets under uniform emission flux.
Distance decay is only qualitative ('within a few tens of meters'); no concentration by height and no stroller height in the main text.

The ELCR is a modelled indicator using a composite slope factor from trace-metal composition of traffic particles; the paper says UFP carcinogenic potency is uncertain. The child excess comes from assumed inhalation rate, body weight and deposition, not observed outcomes.

Children's risk appears only as maps/violins and maxima; site-level source-resolved results (Fig. 9) are for adults only. Older people, riders, cyclists, roadside workers and in-vehicle occupants are not modelled.
Peak versus off-peak ELCR differences partly reflect different assumed slope factors (1.0e-3 vs 7.9e-4 kg day/mg), not only concentration.

Domain-average adult ELCR (about 3.2e-5 to 1.3e-4) is well below the maxima (2.2-3.0e-4); in winter most grid points are below 1e-4 (authors, p.11); summer is broader. The large numbers apply to a minority of locations.

The authors' own comparison puts modelled values within the range of other urban UFP studies (2.5e-5 to 2.0e-4), about the same order as indoor cooking (1.01e-4) and far below smoking (2-6e-1); the 'acceptable risk' band is their wording.
The study area is a dense district (71 % building coverage) with elevated expressways and a freeway interchange; results may not transfer to ordinary streets without viaducts.
Even at the worst canyon sites D and E, roughly half or more of modelled adult risk (read from Fig. 9, approximate) came from elevated sources rather than the street.
correctionsToAbstractLevelNotes: 'Children at highest modelled risk' is confirmed, but specifically the 9-year-old (about 4.5e-4 winter, about 6.5e-4 summer maxima); 3-year-olds are lower; the cause is assumed inhalation per body weight and deposition efficiency.

The 'kerbside hotspots' are not scooter-specific: three vehicle classes are modelled with no vehicle-type attribution, and the highest concentrations (65-80 um2/cm3) are near urban roads beneath expressways.
The abstract's 'about 40 um2/cm3' applies to ground-level urban-road emissions only; all-source maxima are 65 (winter) and 80 (summer) um2/cm3 at peak.
Emission factors include non-exhaust sources, which the abstract does not reveal.

Full text adds the PMF statement (traffic-related SA_UFP more than nine times background or cooking/secondary, from authors' earlier study), school and park results (adults only), and off-peak hotspot D above 1.3e-4.
Cancer risk is placed by the authors alongside indoor cooking and other urban UFP studies and far below smoking, and is called an indicator, not a prediction.
No electrification scenario, no vertical profile and no distance-decay table are in the main text.

Uncertainty: none quantified; authors call all ELCR values potential risk indicators.
answersToQuestions: 1. Zhonghe District, New Taipei City; 1.2 km x 1.2 km target area (building coverage about 71 %) within a circular 800 m-radius computational domain (p.2-3). No new field measurements; earlier on-site data from the authors' previous study (a measurement station at the domain centre and a weather station about 100 m away) were used for validation (p.3). Modelled: steady RANS k-epsilon wind field in COMSOL at about 5 m horizontal and about 1 m vertical near-ground spacing, inlet from Datun Mountain station (9.79 m/s from 60 deg winter; 4.30 m/s from 240 deg summer), then size-resolved convection-diffusion for 20-100 nm particles with line-source emissions = traffic counts x tunnel-derived size-resolved EFs (peak 07-09 and 17-19; off-peak 12-14). Validation: dominant-bin wind speed RMSE 0.29 m/s, NMB -3.7 %; direction RMSE below 20 deg at the measurement station and up to 50 deg at the weather station (p.7). Particle fields compared only qualitatively with earlier measurements: relative ordering reproduced, 'modest discrepancies' in absolute values (p.8); no concentration validation statistics in the main text.

2. Sources are grouped by road type (urban roads, expressways, interchanges, freeways) and vehicles into motorcycles, light-duty and heavy-duty (p.6). EFs are size-resolved particles/km for 20-100 nm from a Taipei tunnel experiment (Fig S3), including exhaust and non-exhaust (brake, tyre, resuspension) and initial dilution/cooling (p.6). The main text prints no EF value for motorcycles and no share of UFP emissions or modelled concentration by vehicle class; traffic counts are in Supplement Table S3. The paper does not say whether motorcycles are gasoline or electric and never uses the word scooter. The only motorcycle mention beyond the class is the title of the earlier study (ref 31, 'motorcycle-dominated urban area').

3. Ground-level urban roads: SA_UFP maxima about 40 um2/cm3 at curbside and sidewalk, decaying 'rapidly within a few tens of meters' (p.8); no distance-decay table. Intersections: hotspots from plume convergence (p.8). Domain mean at 1.6 m, peak: 15 (winter) and 31 (summer) um2/cm3, variability about 15; maxima 65 and 80 near urban roads beneath expressways; off-peak maxima about 45 and 60; off-peak means about 10 and 21 (inferred) (p.8). Particle number concentration is not reported in the main text (metric is lung-deposited surface area). No numeric background value; the open park (location C) has mean adult ELCR below 1e-4 (p.12). Height: receptors at 0.9, 1.2 and 1.6 m only; no vertical-decay result in the main text.

4. Intersections: 'pronounced hotspots at major intersections' (p.8); location F, a busy T-intersection, adult winter peak ELCR about 1.7e-4 with urban roads the primary source in all scenarios (p.13). Street canyons: perpendicular wind gives reduced ventilation and vortices, parallel wind channels flow (p.6); canyon-band shape is 'relatively insensitive to seasonal changes' (p.8); at D the canyon under the expressway keeps ELCR above 1.3e-4 off-peak (p.12). Building downwash brings elevated plumes to street level (p.8). A U-shaped courtyard at school B channelled winter urban-road plumes into the courtyard (p.12). No red-light queue, idling or signal modelling; arcades (covered walkways) are not discussed.

5. Method: ELCR = (IR x T / BW) x SFm x Cf x SA_UFP (Eq. 16), after Sze-To et al. (ref 5); SA_UFP = sum of PNC x deposition efficiency x pi d^2 over 20-100 nm. SFm 1.0e-3 (peak) and 7.9e-4 (off-peak) kg day/mg from the trace-metal composition study (ref 51); Cf 6.6e-13 mg/nm2; MPPD Age-Specific 5-Lobe deposition for ages 3, 9, 21; IR from MPPD defaults, BW from US EPA Exposure Factors Handbook (Table S5); T not stated in main text. Assumptions: size constant, uniform emission per line source, spherical particles, coarse particles negligible. Results: adult max 2.2e-4 winter, 3.0e-4 summer; 9-year-old max about 4.5e-4 and about 6.5e-4; 3-year-olds lower than 9-year-olds; adults lowest; domain-mean adult 3.2e-5 to 1.3e-4. No older-adult group; no confidence intervals. Authors: 'potential risk indicators rather than direct predictions of cancer incidence' (p.11); carcinogenic potency 'remains subject to scientific uncertainty' (p.11); 'potential risks under the assumed scenarios' (p.13).

6. No electrification and no explicit traffic-reduction scenario. Comparisons are season, peak versus off-peak (average emission intensity about 28 % lower off-peak, domain-mean SA_UFP about 32 % lower, local reductions above 35-40 % near major urban roads, smaller in well-ventilated downwind sectors; p.8, 10) and source type. Authors: reducing traffic emissions is 'the most direct way to improve air quality and lower exposure' (p.13). No child-specific scenario results at schools.

7. Limitations (p.13): steady winds; no particle microphysics; 20-100 nm window with total UFP number 'likely underestimated'; ELCR 'rely on a composite cancer slope factor derived for traffic related ultrafine particles in Taipei and on simplified exposure assumptions'; 'detailed time activity patterns, indoor-outdoor penetration and individual susceptibility were not resolved'; to be read 'as potential risks under the assumed scenarios... rather than as precise predictions of absolute cancer incidence'. Also p.11: 'the carcinogenic potency of UFPs remains subject to scientific uncertainty'; p.2: UFP carcinogenicity evidence 'more limited and less consistent than for PM2.5'. The paper does not say in so many words that no regulator has set a UFP cancer unit risk.

8. Can fairly say: in a modelled dense Zhonghe area, lung-deposited UFP surface area at 1.6 m is highest beside busy ground-level roads (about 40 um2/cm3 at kerbs from urban-road traffic alone), with domain means 15-31 and maxima 65-80 um2/cm3 at peak hours; it falls within a few tens of metres of the road; intersections and canyons under elevated roads are modelled hotspots; for the same air, the 9-year-old's modelled lifetime excess cancer risk indicator is about twice an adult's (maxima about 4.5-6.5e-4 versus 2.2-3.0e-4), owing to inhalation per body weight and lung deposition; cutting emissions about 28 % cut mean exposure about 32 %; traffic dominates local SA_UFP (earlier PMF, more than nine times background); a single monitor would miss hotspots. Cannot say: that scooters or motorcycles produce any stated share; that tailpipe exhaust alone produces these values; anything about electrification; red-light queues or idling; stroller-height, elderly, rider, cyclist or roadside-worker exposure; measured concentrations or health outcomes; that anyone's cancer risk 'is' 2e-4 or 6.5e-4; that particle concentrations were validated with stated statistics. Label any risk number 'modelled maximum, adult or child receptor, one Zhonghe district' with the authors' caveat. Suggested wording: 'A 2026 computer-model study of a dense Zhonghe district found the highest ultrafine-particle exposure beside busy roads and intersections, with children at the highest modelled risk; the authors stress the risk figures are indicators, not predictions.'
